passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of three different dietary supplements on the recovery time of athletes after a standardized high-intensity exercise protocol. The study recruited 90 healthy adults aged 20–35, randomly assigning 30 participants to each of three groups: Group A received Supplement X, Group B received Supplement Y, and Group C received a placebo. All participants performed the same treadmill run until volitional fatigue, after which their recovery time was measured as the duration required to return to baseline heart rate and perceived exertion. Blood samples were taken pre- and post-exercise to assess markers of muscle damage (creatine kinase, CK) and inflammation (C-reactive protein, CRP). The table below summarizes the mean recovery times (in minutes) and the mean changes in CK and CRP levels for each group. The researchers hypothesized that Supplement X would reduce recovery time and inflammatory markers more effectively than Supplement Y or placebo.
stem: According to the table, which group had the smallest post-exercise rise in C-reactive protein (CRP)?

options.D: All groups had the same reduction

explanation: The table shows ΔCRP (post-exercise increase) of 1.8 mg/L for Group A, 2.5 mg/L for Group B, and 3.9 mg/L for Group C. Group A had the smallest rise, i.e. the least exercise-induced inflammation.
trap: Reading a higher ΔCRP as a better outcome; a larger post-exercise rise reflects more inflammation.

stem: Which experimental design element best controls for individual differences in baseline fitness levels?

options.A: Random assignment of participants to groups
options.C: Measuring baseline CK and CRP levels
options.D: Providing all participants with identical nutrition plans

explanation: Random assignment distributes individual differences such as baseline fitness evenly across groups, reducing bias. The other options address protocol standardization, baseline marker assessment, or nutrition but do not directly control for fitness variability.
trap: Confusing protocol standardization (B) with randomization as the primary control for individual differences.

stem: If the total post-exercise rise in CK across all participants in Group A is 1,356 U/L, what is the average rise per participant?
explanation: Average rise per participant = total rise ÷ number of participants = 1,356 ÷ 30 = 45.2 U/L, which matches the table’s ΔCK value for Group A.
trap: Using the wrong denominator or averaging across groups, which produces a value that does not equal 1,356 divided by the 30 participants in Group A (45.2 U/L).

stem: Which of the following statements is a common misinterpretation of the study’s findings?

options.A: Supplement X had the shortest mean recovery time.
options.B: The placebo group had the longest recovery time.
options.C: All supplements reduced CK levels equally.
options.D: CRP levels increased after exercise in all groups.

explanation: ΔCK values (post-exercise rises) were 45.2, 58.9 and 72.4 U/L for Groups A, B and C, so the supplements did not blunt the CK rise equally; Supplement X blunted it most. Saying all supplements had equal effects is a misinterpretation.
trap: Assuming equal effectiveness across supplements because every group showed some CK change.

stem: If the three groups were compared with three separate pairwise t-tests each at α = 0.05 (assume independent tests), what is the approximate probability of at least one false-positive result?
explanation: Familywise error = 1 - (1 - 0.05)^3 = 1 - 0.857 = 14.3%. This inflation of type I error is why ANOVA with post hoc correction is used for three or more groups.
trap: Option B (9.8%) is the value for two tests; option A ignores multiple comparisons.
